strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: single-forward, pose-free 3D stylization that scales from a single image to hundreds of views, in contrast to per-scene optimized baselines (StyleRF, StyleGaussian) and view-limited concurrent work (Styl3R).

The architectural design—retaining self-attention for geometry while injecting style via global cross-attention—is a clean and well-motivated adaptation of the VGGT backbone, with an ablation (Table 1, Fig. 2) that convincingly shows global-only coupling outperforms frame-only and hybrid variants.

The proposed voxel-based 3D style loss is a sensible and well-explained extension of BN-statistics style losses into 3D, and the progression from image-level to scene-level to 3D loss is clearly presented with supporting ablations (Table 2, Fig. 3) showing improved short/long-range consistency.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across CO3D (category generalization) and DL3DV-10K/Tanks-and-Temples (scene generalization), including cross-view consistency metrics (LPIPS/RMSE) and a reference-free artness metric (ArtScore), with favorable comparisons to StyleRF and StyleGaussian despite being zero-shot.
Reasonable analysis of scalability/efficiency with respect to number of views (Fig. 4, Fig. 6), giving practical insight into the method's operating range (quality degrades beyond ~32 views).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contribution largely combines existing components (VGGT backbone, AdaIN/BN-statistics style losses, cross-attention conditioning à la AdaIN) rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms; the 3D voxel loss is a natural but fairly straightforward extension of scene-level aggregation.

The comparison against StyleRF/StyleGaussian is not fully apples-to-apples: these are per-scene optimized methods evaluated with released weights, while Stylos is zero-shot; a discussion of the inherent trade-off (e.g., runtime/quality trade-off, or fine-tuned Stylos per-scene as an upper bound) would strengthen the claims.
The most relevant concurrent method, Styl3R, is not empirically compared due to code unavailability, leaving the paper without a comparison to the closest competing approach.

Stylization quality itself is not directly measured by strong quantitative metrics; PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS in the ablation table (Table 1) actually measure content/geometry reconstruction fidelity (using color-jittered/self-reference as style), not stylization effectiveness, which is a somewhat indirect proxy for the paper's central claims about style-content coupling.
No user study is conducted to assess perceptual stylization quality, an important complement to the automatic ArtScore/consistency metrics typically expected in style-transfer papers.

The degradation phenomenon with more than 32 views per batch is only qualitatively described (Fig. 4) without deeper analysis or a proposed mitigation, leaving an important scalability limitation unresolved.

Reproducibility is limited at submission time: code is promised only upon acceptance, and some architectural components (Gaussian Adapter, 3D Fusion module) are only briefly described in the main text without full implementation detail.

Evaluation scenes/categories are relatively narrow (a handful of CO3D categories and 4 Tanks-and-Temples scenes), and it is unclear whether the CO3D ablation scenes were seen during training or held out, raising questions about the ablation's fairness.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: single-forward, pose-free 3D stylization that avoids costly per-scene optimization, which is a meaningful departure from prior optimization-based 3DGS/NeRF stylization methods.

The architectural idea of keeping geometry prediction on a self-attention pathway (inherited from VGGT) while injecting style only via a separate global cross-attention pathway is a clean and sensible design that cleanly disentangles geometry from appearance.

The paper provides a reasonably thorough ablation on style-content coupling strategies (frame/global/hybrid) and on the proposed voxel-based 3D style loss versus simpler 2D/scene-level variants, with both quantitative metrics and qualitative figures.
Demonstrates scalability from a single view to dozens/hundreds of views, which is uncommon among the cited 3D style-transfer baselines (e.g., Styl3R is limited to 2-8 views).
Reasonably broad experimental coverage across CO3D (category-level) and DL3DV/Tanks-and-Temples (scene-level) generalization settings.
weaknesses: The most relevant and recent concurrent competitor, Styl3R, which tackles essentially the same problem (instant feed-forward 3D stylization), is not compared against at all because its code was unavailable; this leaves the central claim of superiority over the closest related work entirely untested.

The quantitative gains from the proposed 3D voxel-based style loss over the simpler scene-level/image-level losses are very marginal (e.g., Table 2: short-range LPIPS 0.046 vs 0.046/0.048, RMSE differences of ~0.002-0.004), which weakens the claimed significance of the main technical contribution.

Baselines used for the main comparison (StyleRF, StyleGS) are per-scene optimized and conceptually quite different from Stylos's feed-forward, zero-shot setting; this comparison is somewhat apples-to-oranges and does not include any other feed-forward Gaussian splatting stylization or naive baselines (e.g., simply applying 2D AdaIN/StyleGaussian-like loss on top of AnySplat, upon which this work is built).

Evaluation is limited in scale: CO3D ablations use only 3 held-out categories, and the Tanks-and-Temples comparison uses only 4 scenes, with no error bars, statistical significance testing, or user study to corroborate the automatic metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, ArtScore) which can be unreliable proxies for perceptual stylization quality.

ArtScore results show large unexplained swings (e.g., StyleGS scores 0.78 on Train but 8.63-9.38 on other scenes), raising concerns about metric robustness or evaluation protocol issues that are not discussed.

The method depends heavily on the pre-existing VGGT backbone (kept entirely frozen/unchanged) and AnySplat's voxelization scheme, and the core technical novelty is incremental: largely a combination of existing feed-forward reconstruction (VGGT/AnySplat) with a relatively standard AdaIN-style statistics loss extended to voxel space and cross-attention-based style conditioning, limiting the paper's originality.

Important training details are missing or only in pseudo-code form (e.g., specific loss weights, learning rates, number of training iterations/epochs, exact size of training data per stage), and code is not yet released, which harms reproducibility despite the stated plan to release it later.

Limitations around generalization are only lightly explored: the observed quality degradation beyond 32 views is mentioned but not systematically analyzed or mitigated, and there is no discussion of failure cases on style types (e.g., highly abstract/non-photorealistic styles) or content domains outside the tested datasets.

The writing in the abstract/intro overstates generality ("generalizes to unseen categories, scenes, and styles") while the experiments test fairly narrow domains (CO3D object categories, DL3DV/Tanks-and-Temples outdoor-ish scenes, WikiArt styles), so the claimed broad generalization is not fully substantiated.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practical problem: single-forward (feed-forward) 3D style transfer without per-scene optimization or precomputed camera poses, scaling from single images to large multi-view collections.

Clean architectural design that cleanly separates geometry (self-attention backbone, unchanged from VGGT) from style conditioning (global cross-attention Style Aggregator), which is intuitive and well-motivated.

The proposed voxel-based 3D style loss is a sensible and novel extension of classical 2D AdaIN/BN-statistics losses into 3D voxel space, and the paper provides a clear progression from image-level to scene-level to 3D-level losses with supporting ablations.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (style-content coupling strategies, style loss variants) with both quantitative metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, short/long-range consistency) and qualitative visualizations.

Comparisons against representative per-scene optimization baselines (StyleRF, StyleGS) on Tanks and Temples show consistent improvements in consistency metrics and ArtScore, despite Stylos being evaluated zero-shot.
Good reproducibility effort via loss pseudo-code, dataset descriptions, and promise of code release; extensive appendix with qualitative results across many style-content pairs.
Efficiency scaling analysis (runtime/memory vs. number of views) provides useful practical insight into the method's deployment characteristics.
weaknesses: The most directly comparable concurrent method, Styl3R (also a shared/disentangled-encoder feed-forward 3D stylization approach), is not compared quantitatively or qualitatively due to code unavailability, leaving a significant gap in validating the paper's central claims against its closest competitor.

Baselines used (StyleRF, StyleGS) are per-scene optimization methods, which is an inherently unfair comparison in favor of the proposed feed-forward model; no feed-forward stylization baseline (e.g., AnySplat-based stylization) is included despite the method building directly on AnySplat/VGGT.
No direct runtime/latency comparison against StyleRF/StyleGS is reported, despite "instant" stylization and avoidance of per-scene optimization being a key claimed advantage.

Reconstruction quality (PSNR 19-22 dB on CO3D) is relatively modest and not clearly contextualized relative to the underlying VGGT/AnySplat reconstruction backbone without stylization, making it hard to assess how much fidelity is sacrificed for style.

The qualitative/quantitative view-scaling study reveals quality degradation beyond 32 views, which somewhat undercuts the abstract's claim of scaling smoothly "from single view to large-scale multi-view settings."

Technical novelty is incremental: the core architecture largely reuses the VGGT backbone and AnySplat's voxelization/Gaussian adapter, with the main new contributions being a cross-attention conditioning branch and a voxel-space style loss, both relatively straightforward extensions of existing techniques (AdaIN, VGGT alternating attention).

No user study or human perceptual evaluation is included to validate style quality and artistic fidelity, relying instead on ArtScore and consistency metrics that may not fully capture subjective stylization quality.

Ablation studies are conducted only on CO3D (object-centric, bounded scenes); it is unclear whether findings (e.g., global vs. frame-level coupling) generalize equally well to larger, more complex scenes like those in DL3DV/Tanks and Temples.
Code is not yet available at submission time, limiting independent verification of claims despite the detailed pseudo-code provided.

strengths: Addresses an important practical limitation of prior 3D stylization work: eliminating per-scene optimization and pose requirements via a single-forward Transformer built on VGGT/AnySplat, enabling instant stylization from unposed images.

Introduces a reasonably novel voxel-based 3D style loss that extends 2D BN/AdaIN-style statistics into 3D voxel space, providing a principled way to enforce cross-view consistency beyond simple per-frame or concatenated-feature losses.

Thorough architectural ablation comparing frame/global/hybrid cross-attention coupling strategies, with both quantitative (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) and qualitative support for the chosen global-attention design.

Strong empirical results on cross-view consistency metrics (short/long-range LPIPS and RMSE) against multiple recent baselines (StyleGaussian, G-Style, StylizedGS, SGSST, Styl3R), and competitive ArtScore/ArtFID with dramatically faster stylization time (0.05s vs minutes for optimization-based methods).
Demonstrates good generalization: zero-shot performance on unseen categories (CO3D held-out classes), unseen scenes (DL3DV→Tanks&Temples), and unseen styles (50 held-out WikiArt/DELAUNAY images).
Additional capabilities such as multi-style interpolation/blending and continuous content-style trade-off control are demonstrated without extra optimization, showing practical flexibility.
Extensive appendix with implementation details, efficiency scaling analysis, and an honest limitations/failure-case section, aiding reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a combination/adaptation of existing components (VGGT backbone, AnySplat voxelization, StyTR2-style CrossBlock, AdaIN/BN-based style statistics), with the 3D voxel loss being an incremental extension of prior 2D and scene-level losses rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Quantitative gains of the proposed 3D voxel loss over the simpler scene-level loss are very small and possibly within noise (Table 2: e.g., 0.047 vs 0.047 LPIPS short-range, 0.153 vs 0.156 long-range), raising questions about how much the added complexity of voxelization actually contributes versus simply aggregating 2D features across views.

Comparison with the closest contemporaneous baseline (Styl3R) is limited to only 4 Tanks & Temples scenes, and evaluation resolutions differ across methods (256×256 for Styl3R vs 448×448 for Stylos), which could bias efficiency/quality comparisons.

ArtScore/ArtFID results in Table 4 are mixed rather than uniformly favorable—G-Style often matches or beats Stylos on FID/ArtScore—so the claimed 'favorable balance' is only partially substantiated and relies heavily on the speed advantage.
No user study or human perceptual evaluation is included, which is standard for style transfer papers to validate subjective stylization quality claims.

The appendix reveals fairly frequent and varied failure modes (inaccurate reconstruction, hallucinated colors absent from style image, blurry regions), suggesting the method's robustness across diverse real-world content may be more limited than the main results imply.

Performance degrades with increasing view count beyond the training regime (>32 views), and the paper attributes this to VGGT backbone limitations without proposing or testing mitigations, limiting the practical 'scalability' claim.

Ablations are conducted on a small number of CO3D object categories/scenes, limiting confidence that findings (e.g., global attention superiority) generalize broadly across scene types and style categories.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and relatively underexplored problem: feedforward, pose-free, single-pass 3D Gaussian stylization that generalizes across scenes/categories/styles without per-scene optimization, which could substantially improve efficiency over existing per-scene 3DGS stylization pipelines.

The voxel-based 3D style loss is a reasonable and intuitively motivated extension of 2D BN/AdaIN-style statistics matching into 3D feature space to enforce multi-view consistency, and the paper includes a clear progression (image-level -> scene-level -> voxel-level) with ablations showing the voxel loss improves consistency and artistic metrics.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies on content-style coupling strategies (frame/global/hybrid cross-attention) and on the three style losses, with both quantitative metrics and qualitative visualizations.

Comparisons against a decent spread of baselines, including per-scene optimization methods (StyleGaussian, G-Style, StylizedGS, SGSST) and the contemporaneous feedforward method Styl3R, with multiple metric families (reconstruction fidelity, short/long-range consistency, ArtScore/ArtFID).
Large appendix with efficiency scaling analysis, detailed failure-case taxonomy, reproducibility details, and extensive qualitative examples, which aids transparency.

Demonstrates auxiliary capabilities such as style interpolation/blending and controllable content-style trade-off without additional optimization, suggesting some practical flexibility beyond the core stylization task.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is largely combinatorial/incremental: the geometry backbone is unchanged VGGT, the voxelization/fusion scheme is taken directly from AnySplat, the cross-attention block is adapted from StyTr2, and the training losses (feature statistics, CLIP, TV) are standard 2D style-transfer losses from ArtFlow/Li et al. The main new contribution is essentially extending BN-statistics matching to voxel space, which is a fairly small conceptual step.

The main quantitative comparison with SOTA (Table 3/4) is conducted on only four Tanks & Temples scenes, which is a very narrow basis for claims of general superiority in cross-view consistency and stylization quality; CO3D ablations are similarly based on just three single scenes (skateboard, pizza, donut), raising concerns about statistical robustness of the reported gains.

On artistic-quality metrics (ArtScore/ArtFID, and the supplementary FID/LPIPS/CFSD/CM-loss tables), Stylos does not consistently outperform baselines such as G-Style — in several scenes G-Style achieves better FID and comparable or better ArtScore, undermining the claim of superior stylization quality and suggesting the main advantage is primarily speed/consistency rather than visual fidelity.

No user study or perceptual study is included despite style transfer being an inherently subjective/qualitative task; reliance solely on automated metrics (ArtScore, ArtFID, LPIPS/RMSE) is a significant limitation for substantiating claims of 'high-quality' and 'aesthetically pleasing' stylization.

StylizedGS is excluded from the main quantitative tables due to failure cases, and such exclusions (as well as excluding failure cases for fairness) could bias comparisons in Stylos's favor without a fully transparent accounting of how many cases were excluded and why.

The appendix failure-case analysis reveals several notable robustness issues (hallucinated colors, missing geometric details, blurring) that are acknowledged but not quantitatively characterized (e.g., frequency of occurrence), making it hard to assess how often these degrade real-world use.

Performance degrades with large numbers of views (quality drop beyond 32 views, as acknowledged), limiting the paper's own claim of scaling 'from single view to large-scale multi-view settings,' since the degradation is tied to a known VGGT backbone limitation that is not addressed by the proposed contributions.

Minor clarity/technical issues: inconsistent notation in Eq. 3 (Rl_b,v vs Rl_b,s), and the color-jitter 'random content view as style reference' trick in Stage 1 is a reasonable but under-analyzed design choice without ablation on its necessity.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful feed-forward 3D stylization pipeline that removes per-scene optimization and camera pose requirements, a meaningful practical advance over NeRF/3DGS-based stylization methods that require costly per-scene fitting.

The two-pathway design (self-attention for geometry, global cross-attention for style) is a clean and well-motivated architectural choice, backed by a clear ablation (Table 1, Fig. 2) showing global cross-attention outperforms frame-level and hybrid alternatives.

The proposed voxel-based 3D style loss is a sensible and novel extension of 2D AdaIN-style statistics matching into 3D voxel space, and the paper provides a clean algorithmic description (Algorithm 1) along with ablation evidence (Table 2, Figs. 3/8-10) that it improves both consistency and perceptual quality over image- and scene-level variants.

Fairly comprehensive empirical evaluation: cross-category (CO3D) and cross-scene (DL3DV→Tanks&Temples) generalization, comparison against 5 recent baselines spanning zero-shot, per-scene-per-style, and feed-forward categories, plus multiple metric families (reconstruction, consistency, artistic quality, speed).

Good transparency: explicit efficiency/scaling analysis (Fig. 7), an honest limitations section with categorized failure cases (Figs. 11-13), and a detailed reproducibility statement with implementation/training specifics in the appendix.
Additional qualitative demonstrations (multi-style blending, content-style interpolation) showcase practical flexibility beyond the core stylization task.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is somewhat incremental since the geometry backbone, camera/depth heads, and voxelization scheme are directly inherited from VGGT and AnySplat; the core new contributions are essentially the cross-attention style-conditioning branch and the 3D style loss, which could be stated more precisely to calibrate novelty claims.

Quantitative comparison in the main experiments (Tables 3-4) is limited to only 4 Tanks & Temples scenes, which is a fairly small testbed for claims of strong generalization; the ablation study (Table 1-2) is similarly limited to 3 CO3D categories/15 scenes.

The closest feed-forward baseline, Styl3R, is only evaluated under its native 2-8 view regime per the paper's own description, raising questions about whether the comparison in Tables 3-4 is entirely apples-to-apples with Stylos's larger-scale multi-view capability.

ArtFID results are mixed — G-Style often achieves better (lower) FID than Stylos despite Stylos's higher ArtScore — so the claim of consistently superior artistic quality is only partially supported by the quantitative evidence.

No human/user study is included to validate subjective stylization quality, which is typically important for style-transfer evaluation given known limitations of automated metrics like ArtScore/ArtFID.
The paper acknowledges quality degradation beyond ~32 views and instability with very few views, which tempers the headline claim of scaling 'from a single view to hundreds of views.'
Some writing/formatting issues (e.g., inconsistent equation subscripts such as σ(R^l_{b,s}) in Eq. 3) suggest the manuscript could benefit from another proofreading pass.
